about.title: About me
about.p1: I'm Dani, from Palma. I study Web Application Development and, outside class, I build things I need: an app that tells me where to fill up, a workflow that logs my matches for me, or an online store.
about.p2: I learn best with a real problem in front of me. If I don't know something, I look it up, try it and break it until I understand it. I use AI every day as a work tool, and I make sure I understand what I end up publishing.
about.p3: I've been a football referee since 2019 and this season I'm in 3ª RFEF. Refereeing has taught me to decide in a second, to stay calm when nobody agrees with me and to own my mistakes. I bring all of that to teamwork too.

surti.lead: An iPhone app that compares the official prices of the petrol stations near you and tells you which one is really worth it, counting price and distance. It also finds EV chargers and keeps track of what you spend.
surti.problem1: Fuel prices change from one week to the next and from one street to the next. Same car, same day: filling the tank can cost several euros more depending on where you stop.
surti.problem2: Checking petrol stations one by one isn't practical. And the cheapest one isn't always worth it: if it's far away, the detour eats up the saving.
surti.f1: Colour-coded price map. Green is cheap and red is expensive, using the official prices published by the Spanish Ministry.
surti.f2: The best option, calculated. It adds up price and detour and points to the station that really saves you the most.
surti.f3: EV chargers. Nearby charging points, filtered by power.
surti.f4: Price alerts. You set your price limit and get a notification when it drops, even if the app is closed.
surti.f5: Price history. A chart that tells you whether today is a good day to fill up.
surti.f6: Expenses and stats. Every fill-up saved, your average price against the local average, and how much you've saved so far.
surti.f7: Widget. The cheapest station, right on your home screen.
surti.f8: No ads, no account. It doesn't ask for your name, email or phone number.
surti.mine1: The whole project is mine: the idea, the screen design, the development with Expo and React Native, and the Supabase backend.
surti.mine2: I also prepared everything around the app: the landing page, the App Store Connect listing and testing with real users on TestFlight before sending it for review.
surti.l1: Publishing an app is much more than coding it: testing, the store listing, screenshots, legal texts and review.
surti.l2: Having other people use it changes your priorities. What seemed clear to me wasn't always clear to them.
surti.l3: Working with real public data forces you to care about details: how it's shown, how often it updates and what happens when it's missing.

n8n.lead: Every week I get an email with the matches I have to referee. This workflow reads those emails and their PDF attachments, pulls out the match details and logs them in a spreadsheet on its own.
n8n.caption: Workflow diagram. It's my own drawing, not an n8n screenshot.
n8n.problem1: As a referee, I get each appointment in an email with a PDF attached. I used to open every email and write the match down by hand in my calendar.
n8n.problem2: It was a small task, but it came back every week, and getting the time or the pitch wrong is not an option.
n8n.s1: Gmail detects the appointment email as soon as it arrives.
n8n.s2: The workflow reads the attached PDF and extracts its text.
n8n.s3: GPT extracts the match details: my role (referee or assistant referee), category, date, time, location, home team and away team.
n8n.s4: A new row is added to Google Sheets with all the fields.
n8n.mine1: I built the whole workflow in n8n: the Gmail trigger, the PDF reading, the instructions so GPT always returns the same fields, and the writing to the sheet.
n8n.result1: I've used it for two seasons. I stopped copying matches by hand and I have all my appointments in one place, sorted and easy to check.
n8n.l1: For AI to be useful inside a process, you have to ask for a fixed format and check what it returns.
n8n.l2: Automating starts with understanding the manual process well, step by step.
n8n.l3: A small automation you use every week teaches you more than a long tutorial.
shop.lead: Four online stores, two of my own and two for other people. In all of them I adapted the theme with Liquid, connected the supplier and prepared the campaigns.
shop.caption: Home page of one of my stores.
shop.ctx1: There are four stores: two of my own, which I built to learn how e-commerce works from start to finish, and two for other people.
shop.ctx2: A freshly installed Shopify theme almost never fits what the product needs. That's where Liquid comes in.
shop.m1: Themes and sections in Liquid. I adapted the theme and created custom sections for the home page and the product page.
shop.m2: Dropshipping suppliers. I integrated the catalogue and the orders with the supplier.
shop.m3: Meta Ads. I prepared and launched the ad campaigns.
shop.l1: Liquid and how a theme is structured: templates, sections, blocks and settings the store owner can change without touching code.
shop.l2: A store is not just the website. Product, ads, supplier and customer service all have to fit together.
shop.l3: Working for someone else forces you to explain things without jargon and to leave the store ready for them to run on their own.
novu.lead: NovuDigital is my web studio for small businesses: digital menus for restaurants, listings for estate agencies and online stores. I designed and coded its landing page from scratch.
novu.idea1: Many small businesses, like the local bar or the neighbourhood estate agency, still have no website, or have one that doesn't bring them customers.
novu.idea2: NovuDigital was created to offer them custom websites with a simple process and direct contact. The first thing it needed was its own website.
novu.m1: A single page with sectors, the work process, packages, an about section and FAQs.
novu.m2: HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no frameworks, so it loads fast even with poor signal.
novu.m3: Designed mobile first, because that's where most visits come from.
novu.m4: Contact through WhatsApp: each button opens the chat with the message already written.
novu.m5: Its own identity: name, colours and a mascot for the brand.
novu.l1: Writing for people who don't know about technology: short sentences and no technical words.
novu.l2: Organising a page so it leads to one single action: sending a WhatsApp message.
novu.l3: Caring about performance and mobile design from day one, not at the end.
domo.lead: I automated my bedroom with smart devices and set up the ones in a relative's home. It's a home project, but it taught me how to make devices from different brands work together.
domo.where: My bedroom and a relative's home
domo.d1: Shelly Plug S: smart plugs to switch devices on and off.
domo.d3: Alexa, Google Home and Google Nest: voice control and control from the phone.
domo.d4: SmartThings: the app that brings the home's devices together.
domo.mine1: In my bedroom I installed the devices, connected them to the network and created the automations I use every day.
domo.mine2: At a relative's home I did the full setup: adding each device, organising them by room and explaining everything so they can use it without help.
domo.l1: Every brand has its own app and its own way of doing things. The hard part is getting them to work with each other.
domo.l2: You design an automation the same way as a program: a condition, an action and the cases where it can fail.
domo.l3: If the person who is going to use it doesn't understand it, it's no use. Simple wins.
conv.coverAlt: Screen of the image converter, with the settings on the left and the area to drop the images
conv.title: Image converter
conv.card: A web tool to convert, compress and resize images without uploading them to any server: everything happens in the browser.
conv.lead: A web tool to convert and compress images without uploading them to any server. All the work happens in the browser, so the photos never leave the device.
conv.w1: Converts several images at once to WebP, JPG, PNG or ICO.
conv.w2: Compresses and resizes: adjustable quality and size by width, height, fit or percentage, without distorting the image.
conv.w3: Background transparent or a solid colour, plus an option to make one colour of the image transparent.
conv.w4: Before and after with file size, dimensions and savings, and a comparison slider.
conv.w5: Download each image or all of them together in a ZIP.
conv.how1: Each image is drawn on a canvas at its final size and the browser itself returns it in the chosen format. Images are converted one at a time so memory does not fill up.
conv.how2: The browser can't create ICO files, so I write the file header by hand and put a PNG inside.
conv.how3: It is built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no frameworks. It works entirely with the keyboard and has a light and a dark theme.
conv.l1: Working with files in the browser: File, Blob and canvas, freeing the memory that is no longer needed.
conv.l2: Reading and changing the pixels of an image one by one to remove a colour.
conv.l3: Thinking about what can go wrong: files that are not images, formats the browser cannot open, huge images and empty fields.
gast.coverAlt: Balance screen of the shared expenses app, showing what each person in a sample group owes or is owed
gast.title: Shared expenses
gast.card: A web app to split the expenses of a trip or a shared flat and work out who pays whom. Everything is stored in the browser.
gast.lead: A web app to keep track of the expenses of a trip or a shared flat between several people and find out who pays whom to settle up. There is no server: the data is stored in the browser.
gast.w1: Several groups at once, each with its own people and expenses.
gast.w2: Four ways to split: equally, by exact amounts, by percentages or by shares.
gast.w3: Balance for each person: what they paid, what their share was and what they owe or are owed.
gast.w4: Payments to settle up, which can be marked as done.
gast.w5: Export and import a group as JSON and copy a summary to send over WhatsApp.
gast.how1: Internally all money is kept in whole cents, to avoid decimal errors in JavaScript. When an amount does not divide evenly, the leftover cents are handed out one at a time so the total always adds up.
gast.how2: To decide the payments, whoever owes the most pays whoever is owed the most, and this repeats until everyone is at zero. It gives few payments and can be explained in a minute, although it does not always guarantee the fewest possible.
gast.how3: It is built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no frameworks or libraries. The code that does the maths is kept apart from the code that draws the page.
gast.l1: Why you should not do money maths with decimals, and how to avoid it.
gast.l2: Designing a simple algorithm, explaining it step by step and knowing its limits.
gast.l3: Not trusting data that comes from outside: I check an imported file in full before using it.
kan.coverAlt: Kanban board with three columns and coloured cards with labels and due dates
kan.title: Kanban board
kan.card: A Kanban board with cards you can drag with a mouse, a finger or the keyboard. Built with Pointer Events and no libraries.
kan.lead: A Kanban board with columns and cards that you move by dragging with the mouse, with a finger or with the keyboard. There is no server: the board is stored in the browser.
kan.w1: Columns and cards that can be added, edited, moved and deleted.
kan.w2: Drag and drop for cards and columns, with a mouse and on mobile.
kan.w3: Keyboard: Alt + arrow keys move the focused card, and every card has a “Move” button.
kan.w4: Colour labels with names and a due date, with a warning when a card is overdue.
kan.w5: Search, filter by label and export and import the board as JSON.
kan.how1: Dragging is hand-built with Pointer Events, which work the same for mouse and touch. When you pick up a card I leave a gap where it was, the card follows the pointer and the gap moves to where it would land.
kan.how2: On drop, the data changes and the board is redrawn. So that nothing jumps, I record where each card was before redrawing and animate it to its new place. If the system asks for reduced motion, nothing is animated.
kan.how3: It is built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no frameworks or libraries. The board data, the dragging and what you see on screen live in separate files.
kan.l1: Building drag and drop by hand, and why the browser's built-in option does not work well on mobile.
kan.l2: Whatever you can do with the mouse must also be possible with the keyboard.
kan.l3: Animating elements that change place when the page is redrawn.
